You eat quickly, then drag a stool to the pallet. Hesper props Piper's shoulders with a rolled blanket, tells you to wake her if anything changes, and leaves the lamp turned low.

Yes, he has a fever. His skin is hot and dry, and you cool it the way Edda taught you, with a cloth wrung out in well-water, laid on his brow and wrists and the back of his neck, then changed every time it warms. Each time, his breathing eases a little, and you hum low while you work. The kettle keeps the air soft and wet.

The second Medicine check (7) doesn't give you the clearer read you wanted. Hour after hour you watch his lips, his color, and what he coughs up, and every sign points two ways. His lips are pinkish, not blue, which is good. But his breath rattles, and the fever neither climbs nor falls. You can't say with confidence whether he is turning the corner or slipping. I won't invent a certainty you haven't earned.

What you can say is this. Cure Wounds mends injuries and won't touch an illness like this, and the prayer that could end a disease, Lesser Restoration, is a 2nd-level spell you cannot cast yet. So all you have is a cool cloth, steam, honey-water, patience, and your presence. That is what Edda gave dying neighbors, and it has often been enough.

It is twenty past eleven. Piper has taken half a cup of broth and a few sips of water in the last few hours, and he has not worsened. He murmured "Da?" once, half awake, and settled when you answered "Soon." You are tired, but not beyond what the work needs. Hesper looked in at ten and went back to bed.

Your prayers are all untouched, you can't rest properly if you sit up all night, and Greywater waits a morning's walk down the road, with Maud and her shawl. What does Brannoc do?

Hesper props Piper's shoulders with a rolled blanket without a word, then pulls the door to and leaves you the lamp. You sit down on the stool, take the cloth from the basin, and begin.

Yes, he has a fever, a real one. His skin is dry and hot to the back of your hand. You wring out a cool cloth and lay it on his brow, and when it warms you change it. You do it again and again, humming Edda's hymn low.

Medicine (19): this time the look is slow and clear, and it tells you plenty.

His lips are pink, not blue. His nails are pink too, with no dusk in the fingertips, so his blood is finding air. There's no rash on his chest or neck, and no swelling under the jaw. The phlegm in the basin is thick and yellow-gray, with no blood in it and no foul smell. His breath whistles on the out-breath but moves in both sides of his chest alike. It is an ordinary lung fever, settled low and angry, and it is not the Grey Fever you grew up with, or anything that will run through the inn. It is dangerous in a child of nine, but a boy who is kept cool, steamed, fed broth and kept upright can turn the corner in two or three days. Tonight, the thing he needs most is exactly what you are doing.

Around ten he wakes once, confused, and asks for his father. You tell him Garn is on the road and will be back soon, and he sips water and sleeps again. Hesper looks in twice, once with a hot brick wrapped in flannel, once with nothing but a long look at you, and goes away again.

Sitting up all night means you won't finish a long rest. You are at full strength and all your prayers are ready, so you lose nothing tonight. A night without sleep has no penalty in the rules you play by, but you'll be tired by morning, and the rest will need to wait for another night.

It is twenty past ten. Piper's fever has eased a little, and his breathing is steadier. What does Brannoc do?

I'll check his breathing and brow every hour or so, humming low. DM: does Piper have a fever I could cool with a damp cloth, and can I try Medicine again with more time, or does anything in the room, like the phlegm or his lips, give me a clearer read?

entries.text:
Hesper props Piper up with a rolled blanket, tucks a second one around his legs, and goes grumbling back to her kitchen with a promise to wake you if anything changes. You eat your bread and stew standing by the pallet, then settle onto a stool with the kettle steaming at your elbow, and hum Edda's hymn low and slow.

Your questions: yes, he has a fever, and you cool it with a damp cloth across his brow and neck, changed every few minutes. You can try Medicine again, because you've now had time. I'm allowing the second check as a new look with new information.

Medicine (20): this time the picture is clear. His lips are pale but not blue, which means he is still getting air. The phlegm in the cup by the bed is thick and yellow-gray, with no blood and no foul smell. The fever is high but even, with no wandering, no rash, no swelling in the neck. This is a lung fever from an ordinary chill that settled low in the chest. It is not a plague, and nothing here is spreading. It needs what you're already giving him: steam, fluids, cool cloths, and sleeping upright. It should break in two or three days, and the danger is that a small body grows tired. Spells wouldn't mend it, since Cure Wounds heals injuries, not sickness, and you don't need to spend a prayer. Rest and care are the cure.

So you sit. You check his breathing and his brow every hour, and he wakes twice for sips of honey-water and calls you "Mam" once before he sleeps again. The kettle sings. Past midnight his breathing eases to a longer, steadier drag, and the whistle goes out of it.

One thing to note as the DM: a night sitting up counts as light activity for a rest, but not as a full long rest. You are at full HP and all your prayers, so it costs you nothing today, but it will leave you tired in the morning. It's about 9 PM now. Do you sit through the whole night, or sleep a few hours and let Hesper take a watch?

sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. I spend the last of the evening kneeling at the plain stone altar, thanking the gods for Piper's mending, Osric's arm, and little Tessa's easy sleep, and humming Edda's hymn until Wren drowses off on the bench with her yarn basket in her lap. Then I lay out my pallet and let the long rest take me.

For tomorrow I'll keep my list as it is: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. I'll go down to Stonebridge in the morning to find Mother Aldith for Perrin and Wren, and keep my eyes open for the next place with no healer.

entries.text:
You kneel at the plain stone altar, give your thanks, and hum until Wren is asleep on the bench with her basket in her lap. Then you lay out your pallet and let the rest take you. The chapel is quiet all night. Nothing wakes you.

It is a little before five on Day 5, and the long rest is done. You're at 17 of 17 HP with all three 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity restored. The list you keep is Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready.

Gray light is coming through the chapel's one window, and the river is loud at the weir. Wren is stirring on her bench, and she sits up fast, remembering, and checks the letter in her sleeve. Down the lane a door opens. Ilsa is at her step with Tessa, and she lifts a hand to you. The baby is awake and pink and fussing for the breast, which is a good sign.

Stonebridge is a day's walk down the valley. You can leave now and arrive by evening, or stay a little longer and see the village's sick once more. You carry honey, a loaf, 15 gp, and a letter for Mother Aldith. The Reach and the Lamp are behind you, and the road runs on. This is the end of the first great chapter of the story. Brannoc has come far, and the game is yours to take wherever you wish.

entries.text:
You sleep on the chapel's stone flags, and nothing wakes you. At 4:50 you open your eyes to a gray window and the smell of old incense, and you feel it settle: all three slots, Channel Divinity, full hit points, and both Hit Dice. Your list is as you chose.

Wren is already up. She has swept the chapel and put the wildflowers in fresh water. She looks tired and pleased, and she has Maud's yarn basket on her hip as if she were going somewhere. She says Ilsa's baby slept through the night, that Osric's dressing has been changed once, and that her mother has said she may go to Stonebridge if you will take her letter and see her safely there. Her mother stands behind her in the doorway, a plump, wary woman with dyed hands, who gives you a short nod and no more.

Maud comes down the lane before you have finished your bread, bundled in a shawl and carrying a basket of her own. It holds a round of cheese, a flask of the river's cold water, and a small parcel wrapped in blue wool. "A blanket for Aldith," she says. "She'll know it's from me. Tell her Maud says she's to be kind to the girl, and that I know where she lives."

It is dawn on Day 5, with Stonebridge a day's walk down the valley. You have a girl who wants to learn, a mother who is trusting you with her, a bonesetter with a sharp tongue, and a road in good weather. Perrin's hip, Wren's apprenticeship, and the next village without a healer all wait down it.

Osric's dressing has been changed already, she says, and Ilsa's baby fed twice in the night. Beyond the door the first gray light is coming up over the weir, the dye racks are dim shapes, and a cock is crowing somewhere down by the river.

Stonebridge is a day's walk down the valley road, and the walk is easier with company. Wren is twelve, her mother has said yes, and the road is not known to you. What does Brannoc do?
